Based on the resource type, you can choose to:\\n\\n * Use automated agent configuration, where GuardDuty manages the agent deployment and automatically creates a Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC)\\n endpoint.\\n * Install agent manually, which requires you to create the VPC endpoint as a prerequisite.\\n\\n The security agent uses a VPC endpoint to deliver events to GuardDuty, ensuring that the data remains\\n within the AWS network. This approach enhances security and allows GuardDuty to monitor and analyze runtime behavior\\n across your resources (Amazon EKS, Amazon EC2, and AWS Fargate-Amazon ECS). GuardDuty uses Instance identity roles that authenticate the security agent for each resource type\\n to send the associated runtime events to the VPC endpoint.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nGuardDuty analyzes runtime events in your AWS environment, uses them internally for threat detection, and presents the results through findings.\\n\\nWhen you manage the security agent (either manually or through GuardDuty) in EKS Runtime Monitoring\\nor Runtime Monitoring for EC2 instances, and\\nGuardDuty is presently deployed on an Amazon EC2 instance and receives\\nthe Collected runtime event\\ntypes from this instance, GuardDuty will not charge\\nyour AWS account for the analysis of VPC flow logs from this Amazon EC2 instance. This helps GuardDuty avoid double usage cost in the account.\\n\\nThe following topics explain how enabling Runtime Monitoring and managing GuardDuty security agent works\\ndifferently for each resource type.\\n\\n###### Contents\\n\\n* How Runtime Monitoring works with Amazon EKS clusters\\n* How Runtime Monitoring works with Amazon EC2 instances\\n* How Runtime Monitoring works with Fargate (Amazon ECS only)\\n* After you enable Runtime Monitoring\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/how-does-runtime-monitoring-work.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Intelligent Threat Detection \u2013 Amazon GuardDuty FAQs \u2013 Amazon Web Services\",\"context\":\"#### Will I incur GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring charges if I don\u2019t use Amazon EKS, Amazon ECS, or Amazon EC2 and I turn on GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for one of those workloads?\\n\\nYou will not incur any GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring charges if you have GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring enabled for a workload that you are not running. However, when you start using Amazon EKS, Amazon ECS, or Amazon EC2 and GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is enabled for that workload, you will be charged when GuardDuty automatically monitors your clusters, tasks, and instances and generate findings for identified issues\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/guardduty/faqs\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Monitoring GuardDuty Usage and Estimating Costs\",\"context\":\"## Understanding GuardDuty Usage\\n\\n### GuardDuty Event Processing\\n\\nWhen enabled, GuardDuty automatically consumes events and logs directly from the log sources in your selected AWS Region. GuardDuty ingests events from separate, independent data sources to provide comprehensive security value.\\n\\n**Important:**\\n\\nYour individual service log configuration or filtering rules (for VPC Flow Logs, DNS Logs, CloudTrail Events, S3 Data Events, Kubernetes Audit Logs, and Lambda Network Logs) do not impact the logs/events processed by GuardDuty.\\n\\n### GuardDuty VPC Flow Logs processing charges for instances monitored by GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring\\n\\nFor instances monitored by GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring (via either EC2 Runtime agent or Amazon EKS Runtime agent), GuardDuty will not charge for VPC Flow Logs processing as long as the agent actively sends runtime event data. If the agent stops transmitting event data, GuardDuty reverts to charging via VPC Flow Logs.\\n\\nEnabling Runtime Monitoring decreases VPC Flow Logs usage in GuardDuty Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics. Disabling Runtime Monitoring restores VPC Flow Logs usage\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/monitoring_costs.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Look up AWS docs on GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring billing when agent isn't transmitting."}

{"id": "34617419-4e5c-4424-9860-069761e7d48f", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "That confirms the mechanism. Here's the breakdown:

**The cost-and-coverage problem**

GuardDuty gives you a VPC Flow Logs billing discount *only* while the Runtime Monitoring agent on an instance is actively transmitting event data. The moment the agent stops sending events — even though "Runtime Monitoring" shows as **ENABLED** at the account/detector level — two things happen simultaneously:

1. **Coverage gap**: GuardDuty loses runtime-based threat detection (process execution, file access, network activity at the OS level) for that instance. You still get some detection via VPC Flow Log analysis, but you lose the deeper runtime visibility you're paying Runtime Monitoring for.
2. **Cost regression**: GuardDuty silently reverts that instance to full VPC Flow Logs processing charges, since the "agent actively sending data" condition that suppresses double-billing no longer holds.

So the account-level toggle being "Enabled" is misleading — it only reflects that GuardDuty is *willing* to accept agent data, not that agents are actually installed, healthy, and transmitting. If most of your EC2 fleet has the agent silently stopped/uninstalled/misconfigured, you're paying for both the Runtime Monitoring feature *and* the standard VPC Flow Logs analysis on those hosts, while getting weaker detection coverage than the "Enabled" status implies.

**Recommended fix**

- Don't trust the account-level "Enabled" flag as a coverage signal. Check **per-instance agent health** — GuardDuty exposes coverage status (e.g., via `ListCoverage` / the coverage page) showing agent status per EC2 instance (`Healthy`, `Unhealthy`, `Not running`, etc.).
- For instances showing unhealthy/not-running agent status, redeploy or repair the agent — most commonly caused by: the agent package not installed via SSM/user-data, an outage in the automated agent-management path, missing IAM instance-profile permissions for the agent, or the required VPC endpoint being unreachable (security group/route table blocking it).
- If you're using automated agent configuration, verify GuardDuty's managed VPC endpoint is healthy and reachable from the affected subnets — a common silent-failure cause is a security group blocking egress to that endpoint.
- Set up a recurring check (or CloudWatch/EventBridge alert) on GuardDuty coverage status so agent drop-outs are caught immediately rather than discovered later as a billing anomaly.

Want me to check the actual per-instance Runtime Monitoring coverage status in your account to see which instances are affected?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
